source: Ratcliff & McKoon (2008) The diffusion decision model: theory and data for two-choice decision tasks
finding: Speed vs accuracy instructions are explained by boundary separation alone. Difficulty is explained by drift rate.
numbers: Exp 2 (N=14): boundary a=0.109 speed vs 0.152 accuracy; accuracy changed 0-6% while median RT changed 120-200 ms. Exp 1 (N=15): drift 0.042 to 0.369 across 5-50% coherence; accuracy 0.58-0.94.
quote: Currently, diffusion model analyses do not explain how subjects set criterion settings.
limits: Applies only to fast single-stage two-choice decisions (mean RT under about 1000-1500 ms). Authors: diffusion analyses do not explain how subjects set criteria.
agent_relevance: The stopping bound is a free policy knob. Raising it buys a few points of accuracy for a lot of time. Our agent should set the bound by instruction or cost, not by default.

source: Ratcliff & McKoon (2008) - starting point and response bias
finding: Unequal response proportions shift the starting point, not drift. A drift-criterion shift added little.
numbers: Exp 3 (N=17): start point about one third of the way toward the likely boundary; adding a drift criterion shift cut chi-square by about 1%. Systematic misfit in .9 quantile of error RTs.
limits: Fit statistics use subject averages and are for comparison only. Across-trial variability parameters are poorly estimated.
agent_relevance: Prior knowledge of how often an answer is right should move the starting evidence, not the evidence rate. A prior on the answer should lower the votes needed for it.

source: Ratcliff & McKoon (2008) - distribution shape predictions
finding: Drift changes stretch the slow tail of the RT distribution about 4x as much as the fast edge. Boundary changes stretch it about 2:1.
numbers: Quantile ratio .9 vs .1: about 4:1 for drift change, about 2:1 for boundary change. Model needs implicit bounds for response-signal and go/no-go tasks.
limits: Human RT distributions are right-skewed; monkey motion-task RTs are reported symmetric, so the model is not equally fitted across species.
agent_relevance: Hard items produce a long tail of extra samples. A fixed sample cap will cut that tail and hurt only hard items.

source: Ratcliff, Smith, Brown & McKoon (2016) Diffusion decision model: current issues and history
finding: Review of what holds up. Fixed bounds are the default; speed stress moves boundaries, and extreme speed stress can also lower drift.
numbers: Hundreds of participants in 10 studies from 3 labs: the great majority better fit by fixed-bound diffusion (reported by the review). Aging slows RT through wider bounds and longer nondecision time, not lower drift.
quote: The data of the great majority of participants were better described by the regular, fixed-bounds diffusion model.
limits: Page text read only to about 100k of 206k characters. Collapsing-bound support is mostly from primates or primate-tuned procedures.
agent_relevance: Slowness is not low ability. A cautious agent (wide bound) and a weak agent (low drift) look alike in time, but differ in accuracy per sample.

source: Ratcliff et al. (2016) - reward-rate optimality test
finding: People do not reliably set the optimal bound. Reward-rate optimality fails as a description.
numbers: Only with feedback did young adults approach reward-rate-optimal performance; older adults rarely moved more than a few percent from asymptotic accuracy.
limits: No sample sizes given in the review text for this point.
agent_relevance: Even humans need feedback to tune a stopping bound. Our agent should get explicit cost-of-attempt feedback rather than assume it self-tunes.

source: Ratcliff et al. (2016) - median-only fit and brief stimuli
finding: Fitting only the median RT hides misfit. Quantile fits expose it.
numbers: In one dataset the median fit but the predicted .1 and .9 quantiles missed by several hundred ms. A model with drift cut off at 80 ms predicted errors slower than correct, contradicting data.
limits: Single-dataset illustrations.
agent_relevance: Judge a stopping rule on the whole distribution of attempts used, not the mean number of samples.

source: Hawkins, Forstmann, Wagenmakers, Ratcliff & Brown (2015) Revisiting the evidence for collapsing boundaries and urgency signals
finding: Large re-test of rival stopping rules. Fixed bounds win for most humans. Collapsing bounds and urgency win only in some monkeys.
numbers: 9 datasets, 8 studies, 4 labs, 85 humans + 8 monkeys, over 116,000 decisions. Humans: 72/85 fixed, 9 collapsing, 4 inconclusive. Monkeys: 4 collapsing, 2 urgency, 2 fixed. Replication 91 more humans: 64 very strong and 12 strong for fixed, 1 collapsing, 14 undecided. Urgency model preferred in 3/93 subjects.
quote: we identified evidence in favor of the standard model with fixed decision boundaries.
limits: Only 2 monkeys per experiment. Six of 8 monkeys (heavily practised) favoured dynamic bounds; practice may matter. When collapsing was nearly flat it was classified as fixed.
agent_relevance: Do not assume the stopping threshold should shrink with time. Evidence says a constant bound is the default for humans on short tasks; a shrinking bound should be justified by task structure.

source: Hawkins et al. (2015) - robustness checks
finding: Conclusion survived BIC vs AIC, a six-model comparison, and a delayed-feedback replication.
numbers: Without between-trial variability, 6 of 8 monkeys preferred fixed bounds. Delayed-feedback replication with 74 humans (1-2 s delay) did not show withholding strategies.
limits: Authors warn against generalising across paradigm, species or procedure.
agent_relevance: If our agent has a hard deadline, a collapsing bound may still be right even though humans without deadlines do not use one.

source: Voskuilen, Ratcliff & Smith (2016) Comparing fixed and collapsing boundary versions of the diffusion model
finding: Independent test of fixed vs collapsing bounds. Only listed here; page could not be read (browser check).
numbers: not read
limits: Not opened; take no numbers from this line.
agent_relevance: Follow up before citing: it is the main human counterpart to Hawkins 2015.

source: Hato, Schumacher, Radev & Voss (2025) Levy versus Wiener: model misspecification and diffusion parameters
finding: If the noise is heavy-tailed, the standard diffusion fit overestimates boundary separation and underestimates nondecision time.
numbers: 100,000 simulated datasets per model; 500 trials per simulated participant. Boundary recovery R2 .99 (DDM) and .98 (LFM) well specified; .77 when LFM data fitted by DDM. Empirical re-fit (Evans 2017, N=43): speed a=1.26 DDM vs 0.97 LFM; accuracy a=1.96 vs 1.82; mean alpha 1.47 and 1.85.
limits: Bias large only when alpha is well below 2. Direction of boundary bias for full models is inconsistent within the paper. Inter-trial variability parameters poorly recovered even when well specified.
agent_relevance: Reported boundary values depend on the noise model. Do not copy numeric bounds from human fits into an agent.

source: Systematic drift variability study (2026) Can systematic drift rate variability replace random variability in the DDM?
finding: Adding trial-level predictors (word frequency, EEG) greatly improves fit but does not remove the random drift-variability parameter.
numbers: N=132 participants, 20 sessions each, about 3,654 trials per person (PEERS recognition memory). WAIC: standard 114,803; exogenous 88,082; endogenous 58,828; complete 37,537. Target eta 2.55 standard vs 2.26 complete; lure eta 0.65 vs 0.63.
limits: One dataset; noisy EEG regressors (single-window classification about 61-69%); LCA not fitted. Conflicts with Ratcliff 2016 who saw a large drop in eta.
agent_relevance: Part of the item-to-item evidence-rate variance stays unexplained. Repeated samples of one model have correlated errors, so votes help less than independence predicts.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Self-consistency improves chain of thought reasoning in language models
finding: Sampling many reasoning paths and taking the majority beats one greedy chain. Gains rise with number of paths and then flatten.
numbers: Code-davinci-002: GSM8K +17.9, SVAMP +11.0, AQuA +12.2, ASDiv +7.6, MultiArith +3.8 over greedy CoT. Bigger models: +12-18 points on AQuA and GSM8K; UL2-20B +3-6; LaMDA +9-23.
limits: Fixed sample count, no stopping rule. Gain depends on model size and answer-space size. Text read: table rows partly cut by layout.
agent_relevance: This is the accumulate-votes baseline whose cost we are trying to bound.

source: Aggarwal, Madaan, Yang & Mausam (2023) Adaptive-Consistency: Let's sample step by step
finding: A Bayesian stopping rule (Beta posterior that the leader is the majority above 0.95) stops sampling when votes agree. Same accuracy at far fewer samples.
numbers: 17 datasets, max 40 samples, temp 0.7. Math 73.2 SC vs 73.1 AC with 40 vs 13.8 samples (3.3x). Commonsense 66.0 vs 65.8, 15.8 samples. Symbolic 72.8 vs 72.8, 13.1 samples. Code 35.2 vs 35.6, 2.4x. GPT-3.5-turbo 76.4 vs 76.2, 10.0 samples (4.4x); Vicuna-13B 54.0 vs 54.1, 21.7 samples (1.9x). Up to 7.9x (Boolean expressions), under 0.1% mean accuracy drop.
limits: Authors' limitation: if the leader is unstable yet the criterion fires, decisions can be suboptimal. Treats samples as independent. Weak model (Vicuna) saves less.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that an SPRT-like bound on votes works. Savings shrink as the model gets weaker, as the drift picture predicts.

source: Aggarwal et al. (2023) - threshold curve and stopping functions
finding: Raising the confidence threshold gives a smooth accuracy-cost curve. The Beta rule beat random and plain-majority stopping and matched costlier rules.
numbers: At equal average cost of 10 samples, Adaptive-Consistency about 3% higher accuracy than fixed-size SC on GSM8K. Beta rule is about four orders of magnitude faster to compute than Dirichlet or CRP rules with similar accuracy.
limits: Random-stop and majority-threshold baselines were weaker. Threshold chosen once (0.95) across datasets.
agent_relevance: A single global threshold works across tasks. Per-task tuning is optional.

source: Li et al. (2024) Escape sky-high cost: early-stopping self-consistency for multi-step reasoning (ICLR 2024)
finding: Sample in small windows; stop when one window is unanimous. Cuts samples a lot at about equal accuracy.
numbers: Sample reduction: MATH -33.8%, GSM8K -80.1%, StrategyQA -76.8%, CommonsenseQA -78.5%, Coin Flip -84.2%, Last Letters -67.4%. Window 5 (8 for MATH); results averaged over 10 runs. Full SC on MATH at 64 samples costs about 2000 USD via GPT-4.
limits: Savings smallest on hard MATH. Window size is a tuning parameter. Read: abstract, method and setup, not every table.
agent_relevance: A cheap fixed-window rule is nearly as good as a full Bayesian bound; start with it.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Make every penny count: difficulty-adaptive self-consistency
finding: Using difficulty from a pre-sample of a batch lets easy questions stop after one try. Beats the stopping rules above.
numbers: Cost cut vs SC: GPT-4 -65.29% and GPT-3.5-turbo -56.04% on average; vs ESC: -24.81% and -21.86%. On GSM8K, CoT and SC agree on 96.2% of items for GPT-4 and 84.8% for GPT-3.5-turbo (SC sample size 40).
limits: Needs a batch of questions to rank difficulty. Partly read; limitations section not read in full.
agent_relevance: For GPT-4-level models most items need one attempt (the agreement figure). The bound matters mainly on the few hard items.

source: Taubenfeld, Sheffer et al. (2025) Confidence improves self-consistency in LLMs (CISC)
finding: Weighting each sample by the model's own confidence reaches the same accuracy with far fewer samples. Evidence quality, not only count, matters.
numbers: 9 models, 4 datasets. P(True) confidence: cost reduction 41% at 5 samples and 46% at 10 on average; 18.6 SC samples needed to match CISC with 10. Over 40% reduction on average; some cells over 67%. Gemma2-9B on MATH: 8 CISC samples beat 30 SC samples.
limits: Best confidence method was not the best-calibrated one. Gains vary by model family and dataset.
agent_relevance: Votes with strength (log-odds) beat unit votes, as in diffusion models with continuous evidence. Use the model's own verdict as a sample weight.

source: Brown et al. (2024) Large language monkeys: scaling inference compute with repeated sampling
finding: Coverage (any sample correct) keeps rising log-linearly with samples, but majority voting and reward models stop gaining after about 100 samples.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite with DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Instruct: 15.9% with 1 sample to 56% with 250. CodeContests Gemma-2B: coverage up over 300x from 0.02% at one sample. MATH Llama-3-8B: coverage 82.9% at 100 samples to 98.44% at 10,000, while voting plateaus beyond about 100.
limits: 128-problem subsets for GSM8K and MATH. Large gains need an automatic verifier. Read: abstract and intro, not all appendices.
agent_relevance: With a verifier, keep sampling until it passes. Without one, stop near 100 votes: the bound does not buy accuracy past that.

source: Chen et al. (2025) Do not think that much for 2+3=? On the overthinking of o1-like LLMs
finding: Long-reasoning models spend rounds after the answer is already found. Early stopping saves tokens at equal accuracy.
numbers: o1-like models used 1,953% more tokens than conventional ones on '2 plus 3'. Method cut token output by 48.6% on MATH500 while keeping accuracy. 2-4 solution rounds in 76-80% of cases for QwQ-32B-Preview and 59-63% for DeepSeek-R1.
limits: Models QwQ and R1 families at the time. Training-free fix; benchmarks mostly math.
agent_relevance: Models do not stop by themselves when evidence is already enough. An external bound is needed.

source: Yang et al. (2025) Dynamic early exit in reasoning models (DEER)
finding: Probe the model for a trial answer at thought boundaries and exit when it is confident. Shorter chains, equal or better accuracy.
numbers: 11 reasoning models, 10 benchmarks (GSM8K, MATH-500, AMC, GPQA, AIME, LiveCodeBench): chain length -19.1% to -80.1%, accuracy +0.3 to +5.0 points. About 75% of samples contain an early point where exiting gives the right answer.
limits: Training-free; needs a trusted confidence signal. Averages over models hide model-by-model spread.
agent_relevance: Gives a within-chain bound, parallel to between-sample bounds. Overthinking can lower accuracy, not only waste cost.

source: Time spent thinking in online chess reflects the value of computation (2025)
finding: Humans think longer when the expected benefit of more thought is higher and time is cheaper. Concave, sub-linear scaling.
numbers: 519 million moves from 12.49 million 2019 Lichess games, plies 15-75. Slopes 1.76 to 38.7 s per unit benefit, all p<1e-50. Square-root form beat linear (dAIC 3.6e8). Expected benefit explained times better (dAIC 1.9e8). Modest Elo effect.
limits: Predicts faster moves as the clock runs down; humans peak at mid clock. Stockfish depth 15 as ground truth. Not a process model.
agent_relevance: Large-N field evidence that stopping time tracks the value of computing. Supports a value-of-computation stop rather than a fixed N.

source: The limits of metacognitive control during perceptual decision-making: opting out without improving accuracy (2025)
finding: Giving people a skip option did not raise accuracy, though they skipped more when stakes and difficulty were higher.
numbers: Exp1 N=24: accuracy 0.82 basic vs 0.82 skip, p=.482. Exp2 N=26 (penalty -3): 0.83 vs 0.84, p=.566, skip rate 0.090 vs 0.043. Exp3 N=36: no basic vs skip effect, p=.462; skip vs accuracy r about -0.03 to 0.08.
limits: Skipping needed an action under the same deadline, so the meta-decision was costly. No computational model fitted.
agent_relevance: Knowing when to abstain is a separate skill from deciding. Do not expect an abstain option to raise answer quality without calibration.

source: Evans & Wagenmakers (2020) Evidence accumulation models: current limitations and future directions
finding: Review of limits of accumulation models. Listed from the search index only; full text not opened.
numbers: not read
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Follow up for stated limits before relying on any claim.

source: Bogacz et al. (2006) The physics of optimal decision making
finding: Known result: a diffusion model with fixed bound is the continuous form of the sequential probability ratio test and is optimal for fixed-difficulty two-choice trials. Not opened.
numbers: not read
limits: Not opened. Optimality holds only when difficulty is constant and known within a block.
agent_relevance: Mixed-difficulty items need a collapsing bound or a difficulty estimate (as in DSC above). Follow up.

source: Gold & Shadlen (2007) The neural basis of decision making
finding: Review of neural accumulation in LIP and a bound-crossing readout. Not opened this session.
numbers: not read
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Background link only; its monkey data are the source of the collapsing-bound claims tested by Hawkins 2015.

source: Cross-source note: human fixed bound vs LLM adaptive stopping
finding: Humans on short tasks keep a fixed bound (Hawkins 2015), yet the best LLM rules vary the bound with item difficulty (DSC, ESC) and gain.
numbers: Human: 72/85 fixed. LLM: DSC saves a further 24.81% (GPT-4) over ESC; Adaptive-Consistency 3.3x fewer samples on math at -0.1 accuracy.
limits: Synthesis by the researcher, not a measured comparison. Different tasks, different cost structures.
agent_relevance: Use a fixed confidence threshold as default (Beta rule 0.95); add difficulty-aware allocation only on mixed-difficulty batches.
